title: AtlasPay hosted gen API onramp: streaming handshake & retries walkthrough
summary: Redwood AE/SE ran a hosted API demo for AtlasPay focusing on streaming handshake, parameter tuning, and retry patterns. Customer raised concerns about tail latency, cost per token, and SOC2 logs. SE offered a sandbox for runbook testing and to run a short benchmark; action items include sending pricing tiers, security package, and scheduling an engineering trial next week.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-05
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood), Ruth Delgado (AtlasPay CTO), Samir Patel (Lead Eng), Elena Morris (Product), Tobias Klein (Security)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm maya from redwood inference, i'll hand it off to liam for a quick live walkthrough of the hosted generation api and how streaming + retries look in practice
[00:22] Liam: yeah thanks maya, hi ruth, samir, elena, tobias — quick agenda, we'll do a 20 minute demo of a small chat flow with streaming, show params you tweak for latency/cost, then cover retry/handshake patterns and the console optimize hints, and leave time for q's. feel free to interrupt.
[00:40] Ruth: quick note — security is important for us and we need SOC2 plus audit logs. also curious about data retention, we can't have logs with PII persist beyond 30 days.
[00:51] Maya: totally noted, we'll show where audit logs appear in the console and i'll share the SOC2 docs after.
[01:05] Liam: jumping in — i'm going to start from a minimal request: text generation chat endpoint, streaming mode. (screen share) here is a sample curl and then the node example. note: the streaming handshake is the same pattern whether you use hosted or dedicated. 
[01:28] (screen noise, brief pause)
[01:33] Liam: ok sending first request — prompt is a customer support flow, short context then question. you'll see tokens come back incrementally. the server responds with a small chunk, then the rest. watch the intermediate deltas — this is application-level stream, not chunked raw stdout.
[01:54] Samir: can you repeat the param for max latency? we have users in europe so p95 matters to us.
[02:01] Liam: sure — there are a few knobs. max_tokens, response_timeout, and an explicit low_latency flag we expose per-route that biases smaller batch windows. p95 is mainly affected by batching config and KV cache hit rates.
[02:20] Maya: also our smart routing can send EU traffic to regional pools, that helps latency.
[02:28] Elena: how does the handshake work when a stream fails mid-response? we had issues with partial messages.
[02:35] Liam: good question. our client libraries implement idempotency tokens and a resume token in the stream. if the connection drops you can re-open with the same idempotency key and the server will replay from the last confirmed token. sometimes the transcript might duplicate a short tail — we recommend dedupe on the client for final assembly.
[02:58] (brief crosstalk)
[03:05] Tobias: what about replaying when the model variant changes during a rollout? will token counts differ?
[03:12] Liam: yes it can. for rollouts we suggest pinning a model version for a cohort or using fallback policy — we can configure automatic fallback to a compatible quantized variant. the console shows version pins per route.
[03:30] Samir: and cost — if we bias for low latency are we paying more?
[03:35] Priya: usually yes, smaller batch windows mean lower batching efficiency so higher per-token cost. Optimize will recommend a sweet spot given your traffic shape; it can propose batching size and cache TTLs based on your traces.
[03:50] Ruth: can Optimize give hard numbers? we need to model monthly spend for our 10M monthly messages estimate.
[03:58] Maya: we can run a quick estimate — send your traffic histogram and sample prompts, we can run a costing sim and produce a few configs: low-latency, balanced, and cost-optimized.
[04:14] Liam: back to the demo — i'm switching the route to low_latency=true (shows console). notice throughput here drops a bit but p95 goes down several hundred ms. streaming chunks arrive faster, you get shorter first-byte time.
[04:36] Liam: now i'll simulate a transient failure — close the socket, then re-open with the idempotency header. you'll see the server emits a resume token and we continue from the last confirmed token. the client lib logs show a short duplicate which we trim on receipt.
[04:58] Samir: that resume token concept — is that part of the HTTP streaming spec or our client implementation?
[05:05] Liam: it's in our client and server together. the protocol is our streaming layer over http/2 or websocket, we include sequence markers in events. it's not a generic spec but it's stable across our SDKs.
[05:20] Elena: any limitations around long conversations? we may keep 8k of context around.
[05:26] Liam: we support long context up to model limits (depends on model), and we have KV cache to reuse prefixes which reduces compute. but large context increases token processing cost and can raise latency. Optimize suggests partial caching strategies.
[05:44] Tobias: security — where are logs stored and how do we redact? do you integrate with KMS?
[05:50] Maya: yes we support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM for private deployments; for hosted we have envelope encryption and you can request logs with PII redaction. we'll attach the detailed security pack after this call.
[06:06] (screen share continues)
[06:15] Liam: i'm going to show a dev flow: create route -> choose model -> route config (batching TTL, low_latency toggle) -> sample requests. here's the request inspector with token-level cost estimate. note the estimate is an approximation but useful for planning.
[06:38] Samir: the token estimate — is that per-call or averaged over time?
[06:41] Priya: it's per-call projected then rolled up in console usage views. you can run a sequence of sample requests to see expected monthly burn.
[06:53] Ruth: what's the SLA for hosted? we need 99.9 for our payment flows.
[06:59] Maya: hosted has enterprise SLA options when you sign up for higher tiers; Dedicated buys you more predictable throughput and stricter SLOs. we can show a mapping of tiers.
[07:14] Samir: our ideal is to keep most traffic on hosted but have an on-prem option for high-sensitivity flows. is that hybrid supported?
[07:23] Jordan: yes — you can route based on policy: sensitive flows go to Private or Dedicated, everything else stays hosted. routing can be per-route or per-customer.
[07:35] Liam: back to retries — there are three patterns: optimistic retry (client retries automatically with backoff and idempotency key), failover retry (route to fallback model/region), and canary-aware retries (respect rollout pins). we show code for optimistic retry in the node lib.
[07:55] (minor transcription glitch)
[08:02] Samir: if we do optimistic retry with backoff, how do you recommend tuning backoff parameters to avoid thundering herd?
[08:10] Liam: generally exponential backoff with jitter and capped max attempts. also use circuit breakers on the client side. Redwood console exposes health metrics so you can tune retry windows based on observed server load.
[08:24] Elena: can we see a live example of a retry causing duplicate output? want to understand UX implications.
[08:30] Liam: sure — i'll intentionally drop acks to force a client retry, you'll see the client re-request and the server resumes; the client library returns a flag that says resumed=true so apps can choose to append vs replace.
[08:47] (pause)
[08:50] Tobias: one more security nit — audit log retention needs to be configurable to 30 days for us and logs must be exportable to an S3 bucket.
[08:58] Maya: that's supported; we can push logs to your S3 and set retention policies. i'll include the exact steps in the security doc.
[09:10] Liam: quick note about misrecognitions — sometimes service names in transcripts are garbled (re e.g., KV cache might show up as 'k v cache' in auto transcripts). not important for runtime but FYI.
[09:22] Ruth: that's fine — just want to avoid surprises.
[09:27] Maya: wrapping the demo, a few pragmatic suggestions: use small context windows for high-volume chat at first, enable KV caching for repeated prompts, and let Optimize propose batching sizes after 48 hours of traffic.
[09:44] Samir: can Optimize automatically apply changes or just recommend them?
[09:49] Priya: it initially recommends; you can enable auto-apply for low-risk changes like cache TTL adjustments. anything that affects model choice or quantization needs manual approval.
[09:59] Elena: about quantization — we likely want smaller models for cost reasons; does hosted support quantized variants?
[10:06] Liam: yes, we onboard quantized variants and show perf/cost tradeoffs in the model catalog. automatic fallback to quantized variant is possible for heavy load.
[10:19] Ruth: final question — what's the process for a bench test? we'd like to run a simulated traffic spike and measure p95 and cost.
[10:27] Maya: simple: we provision a sandbox route, upload your prompt set and traffic pattern, we run a 2-hour or 24-hour bench and provide a report with p50/p95, token counts, and cost projection. we'll need a few sample prompts and a histogram of request sizes.
[10:44] Ruth: ok we'll prepare that, aim for next wed.
[10:48] Maya: perfect. quick recap of next steps — i'll send pricing and SOC2 pack; liam will provision sandbox and priya will send Optimize docs. any other items?
[10:59] Samir: nothing else, thanks — also can you send the node sdk snippet you used?
[11:05] Liam: yes, will include node and python quickstarts and a small snippet showing idempotency header and resume token usage.
[11:13] Elena: thanks all, this was helpful.
[11:16] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: some speaker labels generic and occasional sentence fragments; auto-transcription mis-heard a couple of product names (e.g., "reduce token" vs "KV cache").
